name: Apricot
lede: Apricot is the soft orange-yellow of the fruit, a name that fashion and the pearl trade have used for a long time and that the old color books mention mostly in passing.

sections.title: The fruit's color
sections.body:
Paterson defines apricot plainly as the orange-yellow of the fruit [1]. Our swatch is a light, warm orange, and its closest named neighbors are [[apricot-buff]], [[light-salmon-orange]] and [[mandarin]], the first two from Ridgway's 1912 atlas and the third a Japanese-derived name [2]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the color in blocks 52 and 53, and lists Golden Apricot and Talisman beside it [2].

Pastoureau makes a quieter point about vocabulary. Medieval yellows, he says, lean toward orange, beige and brown, and from lightest to darkest he would describe them as straw, chamois, apricot, honey, russet, tawny, bister and bronze [3]. Those are his descriptive terms, not a medieval list. He also argues that terms like apricot, pumpkin, saffron and tan cannot replace the word orange, because color words have no true synonyms and each shifts the connotation [4].

sections.title: Where the word turns up
sections.body:
Apricot is a pearl color. Finlay lists the shades of pearls as running from pure white through champagne, apricot, bronze, pink, lavender and grey to black, and, very rarely, green [5]. The nearest gem entry in our data is [[gem:pearl|pearl]] [5].

It was also a fashion partner. In 1880, St Clair reports, the purple dye color heliotrope was paired with light green or apricot, and over the following decade with a run of louder partners, from canary yellow to peacock blue [6]. Finlay, travelling in a high valley beside Kashmir, notes apricot orchards among the few places where bright green fields interrupt the dry earth and glaciers, a reminder that the word started with a tree [7]. The tree is in our botany data as [[flower:apricot|apricot]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Apricot is moderately rare in our painting archive: 67 of 23,781 paintings, 0.28 per cent, and rarer than 53 per cent of the named colors [8]. In the within-painting count of 41 paintings it plays an accent in 63 per cent [8]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 0.4 per cent of the 1,674 paintings from then, 1.7 times the museums' baseline, and our earliest match is a work of 1300 by Giotto, a floor for a thin early archive and not a first [8].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, which tend to yellow and warm every pale color, so an apricot match is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test [8]. In printed English the adjective peaks in the 2010s, after a first rise in the 1920s [8].

origin.first_recorded: as a color name, ISCC-NBS 1955 and Paterson; earlier use undocumented in our sources

disambiguation.gloss: a nearby pale orange from a different fruit, usually a little pinker
